steps_tex: Yes: each animal's length along the speed line stands for its speed, as a bar does.
$(a)$: The marks go up in equal steps of about $16$ kilometres per hour ($10$ miles per hour each).
$(b)$: Answers vary; for example, the peregrine falcon dives at about $322$ kilometres per hour.

$(c)$: Falcon $322$ and swift about $170$ (estimate, accept $160$ to $180$): $322 \div 170 \approx 1.89$, about twice. Sailfish about $109$ and flying fish about $56$: $109 \div 56 \approx 1.95$, about twice.
$(d)$: Estimates from the bars: sailfish about $109$ (accept $105$ to $113$) and humpback whale about $26$ (accept $22$ to $30$): $109 \div 26 \approx 4.19$, so yes, about $4$ times.
But only five water animals are shown, so the graph cannot say the sailfish is the fastest in the world.

steps_tex: With $1\text{ unit} = 4^\circ C$, $20^\circ C$ is $20 \div 4 = 5\text{ units}$ and $43^\circ C$ is $43 \div 4 = 10.75\text{ units}$.
Draw two bars at each time, one for each day.
Day $1$ runs from $16^\circ C$ to $34^\circ C$, a range of $34 - 16 = 18^\circ C$, mean $188 \div 8 = 23.5^\circ C$.
Day $2$ runs from $30^\circ C$ to $43^\circ C$, a range of $43 - 30 = 13^\circ C$, mean $295 \div 8 = 36.875^\circ C$.
Cool nights near $16^\circ C$ suggest winter, for example December or January.
Nights of $30^\circ C$ or more and an afternoon of $43^\circ C$ suggest peak summer, for example May or June.
item.answer_tex: Day $1$ is likely a winter day (December or January) and Day $2$ a summer day (May or June)

steps_tex: $(a)$: The guidelines are at $25000$, $50000$, $75000$ and $100000$. Gujarat's $89000$ lies between $75000$ and $100000$; Delhi's $62000$ lies between $50000$ and $75000$.

item.question: Test the six statements against the table of average heights.
steps_tex: Statement $1$ is justified: at every age both columns are higher in $2019$ than in $1989$, for example age $19$ boys $163.5$ to $166.5$ and girls $151.9$ to $155.2$ (some ages dipped slightly in between, for example boys aged $15$, $155.4$ to $155.2$ from $1989$ to $1999$).
Statement $2$ is not justified: $13$-year-old girls in $1989$ are $143.2$, less than $14$-year-old girls in $2009$ at $148$.
Statement $3$ is justified: $15$-year-old boys in $2019$ are $159$, more than $16$-year-old boys in $1989$ at $158.9$.
Statement $4$ is not justified: averages say nothing about every girl; some $11$-year-olds can be taller than some $13$-year-olds.
Statement $5$ is not justified: girls' averages are higher at ages $11$ and $12$ in every year, for example $2019$ age $11$, $138.6$ against $137$.
Statement $6$ cannot be decided: the table stops at $19$; in $2019$ boys grew only $166.5 - 166 = 0.5\text{ cm}$ from $18$ to $19$.
item.answer_tex: Justified: $1$ and $3$; not justified: $2$, $4$ and $5$; $6$ cannot be decided from the table

Statement 3 is justified: 15-year-old boys in 2019 are 159, more than 16-year-old boys in 1989 at 158.9.
Statement 4 is not justified: averages say nothing about every girl; some 11-year-olds can be taller than some 13-year-olds.

item.text:
$1$. Statement $1$ is justified: at every age both columns are higher in $2019$ than in $1989$, for example age $19$ boys $163.5$ to $166.5$ and girls $151.9$ to $155.2$ (some ages dipped slightly in between, for example boys aged $15$, $155.4$ to $155.2$ from $1989$ to $1999$).
$2$. Statement $2$ is not justified: $13$-year-old girls in $1989$ are $143.2$, less than $14$-year-old girls in $2009$ at $148$.
$3$. Statement $3$ is justified: $15$-year-old boys in $2019$ are $159$, more than $16$-year-old boys in $1989$ at $158.9$.
$4$. Statement $4$ is not justified: averages say nothing about every girl; some $11$-year-olds can be taller than some $13$-year-olds.
$5$. Statement $5$ is not justified: girls' averages are higher at ages $11$ and $12$ in every year, for example $2019$ age $11$, $138.6$ against $137$.
$6$. Statement $6$ cannot be decided: the table stops at $19$; in $2019$ boys grew only $166.5 - 166 = 0.5\text{ cm}$ from $18$ to $19$.
Answer: Justified: $1$ and $3$; not justified: $2$, $4$ and $5$; $6$ cannot be decided from the table

topic_name: Zoomed Charts and a Mean Decision
concept_name: A chart that starts at 145 cm

item.question: On a chart whose axis starts at 145 cm, one marker sits at 165 cm and another at 155 cm. How do their lengths from the axis compare, and how do the heights compare?
steps: Length above the axis: 165 − 145 = 20 and 155 − 145 = 10.
So the first looks 20 ÷ 10 = 2 times as tall.
True heights: 165 ÷ 155 ≈ 1.06, only about 6 percent taller.
The zoomed axis makes a 10 cm difference look like doubling.
Always read the values from the axis, not the lengths.
item.answer: The first looks 2 times as tall, but the true ratio is 165 ÷ 155 ≈ 1.06

topic_name: Zoomed Charts and a Mean Decision
concept_name: A mean decision: a door for the family

item.question: A family's heights are 169, 173, 155, 165, 160 and 164 cm. A door is made at the mean height. Who must bend, and what height should the door be?
steps: Taller than 164.33: 165, 169 and 173, so 3 of the 6 members must bend.
A door must fit everyone, so it must be taller than the maximum, 173 cm, with some room to spare.
item.answer: 3 members must bend; the door should be taller than the maximum, 173 cm
item.text:
Worked example: A family's heights are 169, 173, 155, 165, 160 and 164 cm. A door is made at the mean height. Who must bend, and what height should the door be?
1. Total: 169 + 173 + 155 + 165 + 160 + 164 = 986 cm.
2. Mean: 986 ÷ 6 ≈ 164.33 cm.
3. Taller than 164.33: 165, 169 and 173, so 3 of the 6 members must bend.
4. A door must fit everyone, so it must be taller than the maximum, 173 cm, with some room to spare.
Answer: 3 members must bend; the door should be taller than the maximum, 173 cm
